name: Jade Dubois

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Marc and I bought Hilltop seven years ago, 200 acres that had been let go, and we've been dragging it back ever since. We've got 60 Hereford cows, 200 ewes, some wheat and oats, and we sell beef and lamb boxes straight to customers online. My morning starts with the drone over the top fields to count stock, then whatever's broken, then packing boxes in the cold room on Thursdays. I use AI every day: for the grazing plan, the customer emails, the box website, even for checking a weird-looking ewe before I ring the vet.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Every penny is in the farm. We borrowed for the land, then again last year for the cold room, so we've got maybe ten days of bills in the bank at any time. Marc works four days a week as an agronomist, advising other farms on their crops, and that's what pays the mortgage on the house. The kids, Elodie and Hugo, think we're rich because we own fields. We're not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. I'll read it as written. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be a bit disappointed. I've built half my business on these tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's still worth using, and anyone who ignored it lost nothing but also gained nothing. I'd post about how much time it saves me on the box business. I'd be the one still going on about it at the market.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, the farm's problems are money problems, not AI problems. Beef box orders have dropped by a fifth since prices went up, and the cold room loan payment is fixed. A plateau doesn't fix any of that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push the box business harder: a monthly subscription box, with the AI writing the newsletters and handling orders. I'd sell 15 of the cows this spring to get the loan payment covered through summer. And I'd ask Marc to take on one extra client.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Stretched. Not about AI, about the bank account.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much does the box business bring in?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: On a good month, about four thousand pounds before costs, and costs are most of it. The subscription idea would make it steadier, people paying every month instead of when they remember. I'd test it with fifty customers first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The kids' swimming lessons would go to every other week. We'd skip the summer week at Marc's parents. I hate it, but Elodie and Hugo would survive, kids are tougher than we think.

say: I'd say AI is **still worth using**, and I'd keep showing what it saves me.
I'd be the one **going on about it** at market.
think: I think the farm's problems are **money problems**, not AI problems.
Box orders are down **a fifth** and the cold room **loan** is fixed.
do: Launch a **monthly subscription box**, with AI writing newsletters and orders.
Sell **15 cows** this spring to cover the loan through summer.
Ask Marc to take on **one extra client**.
feel: **Stretched**, about the **bank account** rather than AI.
S0.quote: The farm's problems are money problems, not AI problems.
fieldNote: Jade is a **heavy AI user** whose business depends on online sales.
Her pressure is **debt and falling orders**, with ten days of savings.
She'd respond by **pushing harder**, not cutting back on ambition.
Her partner's **agronomy job** pays the mortgage, a fact that matters later.

steps.text: Launch a monthly subscription beef box with fifty customers
Sell 15 Hereford cows this spring to cover the cold room loan
Cut the kids' swimming to every other week

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Thinking tasks first. That's me laughing and Marc not laughing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a huge chance for small farms that sell direct, because we can do what big firms do with a fraction of the staff. I'd post about it, and I'd run a session at the young farmers. I'd also say people in advice jobs need to think hard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's good for my side and bad for Marc's. Marc's agronomy is exactly the kind of thinking work AI eats: soil tests, crop plans, spray advice. If his clients get an app that does it for a tenth of the price, we lose the money that pays the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd automate the box orders, the customer service and the delivery routes in the first six months. I'd help Marc move into something hands-on that AI can't do yet, maybe soil sampling or running trials in the field. And we'd build the box business up so it could carry more of the house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited for the farm, worried for Marc. Both at once, all the time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does Marc feel about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Marc's quieter about it than I am. He says the advice is only half his job, the other half is walking fields and knowing the farmer. He's right, but the half he does at a desk is the half they pay him for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if Marc's clients dropped off?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Bring him onto the farm and the box business properly. He's good with customers and the farm could use him. The problem is the farm doesn't pay a wage yet, it pays the loan.

I'd warn that people in **advice jobs** need to think hard.

fieldNote: Jade's farm **gains** from Steady Disruption, but her partner's job is exposed.
The household's **mortgage earner** is at risk, which sets her mood.
Her answer is to pull Marc **onto the farm**, though it can't pay a wage yet.
She's clear about the split between **desk and field** in his work.

steps.text: Automate box orders, customer emails and delivery routes within six months
Help Marc move into hands-on soil sampling and field trials
Grow the box business until it can pay part of the mortgage

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: 2028 for the thinking, 2031 for the robots. Marc's job is gone in the first bit, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the government needs to put money into rural areas now, while there's time to build new work. I'd be online saying that farmers who use the tools will survive and the rest need help. I'd say it plainly, without sugar.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, Marc's agronomy work is finished by 2028, so we lose the mortgage money. My side has three years before the robots, and I'd use them to get robots in myself, because otherwise the big farms flood the market with cheap robot-reared beef. It's a race I might win. With ten days of savings, I'm racing in flip-flops.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sign up for a robot fencing and herding trial in the first year, even on a lease, to get ahead. I'd put Marc full-time on the box business and the customers. And we'd look at renting out the farmhouse annexe as holiday lets, which brings in money from people, not machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Terrified and fired up. I can't tell the two apart some days.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do the three years before robots give you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They're my window. Thinking AI arrives and I already use it, so that's no shock. The robots are what changes my side, and if I'm running them by 2031, I'm the one with the cheap beef.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Elodie and Hugo?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my kids Elodie and Hugo that their dad's job changed and we're all going to work on the farm together for a bit. Elodie would want to run the website. Hugo would want to drive the robot.

say: I'd say government must put **money into rural areas** now.
I'd say farmers using the tools survive and **the rest need help**.
think: I think Marc's agronomy is **finished by 2028**, taking the mortgage money.
My side has **three years** before robots to get ahead of big farms.
do: Sign up for a **robot fencing and herding** trial, even on lease.
Put Marc **full-time** on the box business and customers.
Rent out the **farmhouse annexe** as holiday lets.
feel: **Terrified and fired up**, often both at once.
S2.quote: With ten days of savings, I'm racing in flip-flops.
fieldNote: Jade expects her partner to **lose his job** by 2028, taking the mortgage money.
She sees the **three-year robot gap** as her window to get ahead.
Her plan mixes **automation and people**: robots on the farm, holiday lets in the annexe.
Thin savings make her ambition feel **risky**, and she says so.

steps.text: Lease robot fencing and herding kit on a trial in the first year
Move Marc full-time onto the box business and customers
Rent out the farmhouse annexe as holiday lets
Post that government must fund new rural work now

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's enough time to get Marc out of agronomy before it collapses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a gift if we use it. I'd want grants for small farms to buy robots and training for people like Marc. I'd say that online and at the young farmers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel we could do it. Marc gets three or four years of agronomy money while he builds something else. I get time to pay down the cold room loan and pick the right robots instead of the first ones.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get Marc to start a field trials business now, testing new crop varieties for seed companies, which is hands-on. I'd put a little away for a robot deposit, maybe a hundred pounds a month. And I'd keep pushing the box business, with the AI handling everything but the packing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but in the good way, the way you feel before lambing starts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What changes on the farm between 2031 and 2034?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: From 2031 the AI does all my planning, ordering and selling, which it mostly does already. From 2034 robots can do the fencing, feeding and moving. I'd plan to be running both by then, or I'm competing against farms that are.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And if the robots are too expensive?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd share them, maybe with two neighbours. Our neighbour Ruth has the land next door and no kids to take it on. She might go in with us.

S3.quote: Our neighbour Ruth has the land next door and no kids to take it on.
fieldNote: Five years lets Jade **plan Marc's move** before his income disappears.
She'd **share robots** with a neighbour if they're too dear.
Her anxiety is **energising**, but the household income is still at risk.

steps.text: Help Marc start a field trials business for seed companies

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's the one where I'd come out ahead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough to make sure every small farm has a fair chance at the new tools. I'd push for shared robot schemes through the local farmers' group. And I'd keep saying it at every meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think we'd be fine. Marc has time to move out of agronomy slowly, the loan is mostly paid by 2036, and I'd be among the first small farms running robots. The worry is just the usual thin money in between.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the AI tools and the box business going and add robots when the prices come down, probably around 2034. I'd help Marc build his trials work bit by bit. And I'd try to get three months of savings by 2030.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Curious, a bit excited. Not afraid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell other farmers in your area?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them to start small now, one tool at a time, and not wait for the robots to arrive. Every year you wait is a year someone else learns first. I'd offer to show them what I use.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that would still worry you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Prices. If cheap robot beef floods in before I've got robots, we're squeezed. And honestly, if one of us got sick, ten days of savings would be gone in a week.

I'd push for **shared robot schemes** through the farmers' group.
think: I think we'd be **fine**, with Marc moving slowly and the **loan mostly paid**.
The worry is the usual **thin money** in between.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because Marc's job goes before we've built anything to replace it, and we've got ten days of savings. What would help is grants for small farms to get robots early, and a bridge payment for people like Marc while they switch.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask about the partners. Everyone asks about the farmer, but half of farms are kept alive by someone's off-farm job. When the off-farm job goes, the farm goes with it.

headlineQuote: Half of farms are kept alive by someone's off-farm job.

Her partner's **agronomy job** pays the mortgage and is her biggest exposure.
She's **pragmatic**, plans to use robots early, and wants grants for small farms.
Her mood runs **alarmed** in the fastest scenario and **uneasy** with a decade.
